items.readable_text:
Content:
Periodic functions are special functions that repeat themselves every [MATH: c] units. The smallest positive value of [MATH: c] that has this property is called the period of the function.

Content:
Let's take the following periodic function as an example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/297884a427a047f5b0209ac6933e06b2]

Content:
This function repeats itself with a period of [MATH: 2.] To illustrate, first focus on the part of the graph shown in blue below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f553c854f69e02657b402b40469a7078]

Content:
If we shift this part [MATH: 2] units to the right, the graph remains unchanged!

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/90b02afb5183c653fe9bc0e6bff04426]

Content:
The same would happen if we shifted the part [MATH: 2] units to the left.

Content:
By knowing the period of a periodic function, we can use a value of the function to infer many other values of the function. For example, in the function above, note that [MATH: f(4)=0.] Since the period is [MATH: 2,] if we add (or subtract) any multiple of [MATH: 2] from the input, the output stays the same. We can write this as

Content:
[MATH: f(4+2n) = 0,]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is an integer.

Content:
For example, setting [MATH: n=1,2,3\ldots] gives the following:

Content:
[MATH: n = 1: f(4 + 2(1))|= f(6) = 0; n = 2: f(4 + 2(2))|= f(8) = 0; n = 3: f(4 + 2(3))|= f(10) = 0; ⋮]

Content:
The same is true for negative values of [MATH: n.] Setting [MATH: n=-1,-2,-3\ldots] gives the following:

Content:
[MATH: n = − 1: f(4 + 2(− 1))|= f(2) = 0; n = − 2: f(4 + 2(− 2))|= f(0) = 0; n = − 3: f(4 + 2(− 3))|= f(− 2) = 0; ⋮]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Periodic functions are special functions that repeat themselves every [MATH: c] units. The smallest positive value of [MATH: c] that has this property is called the period of the function.

Content:
Let's take the following periodic function as an example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/297884a427a047f5b0209ac6933e06b2]

Content:
This function repeats itself with a period of [MATH: 2.] To illustrate, first focus on the part of the graph shown in blue below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f553c854f69e02657b402b40469a7078]

Content:
If we shift this part [MATH: 2] units to the right, the graph remains unchanged!

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/90b02afb5183c653fe9bc0e6bff04426]

Content:
The same would happen if we shifted the part [MATH: 2] units to the left.

Content:
By knowing the period of a periodic function, we can use a value of the function to infer many other values of the function. For example, in the function above, note that [MATH: f(4)=0.] Since the period is [MATH: 2,] if we add (or subtract) any multiple of [MATH: 2] from the input, the output stays the same. We can write this as

Content:
[MATH: f(4+2n) = 0,]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is an integer.

Content:
For example, setting [MATH: n=1,2,3\ldots] gives the following:

Content:
[MATH: n = 1: f(4 + 2(1))|= f(6) = 0; n = 2: f(4 + 2(2))|= f(8) = 0; n = 3: f(4 + 2(3))|= f(10) = 0; ⋮]

Content:
The same is true for negative values of [MATH: n.] Setting [MATH: n=-1,-2,-3\ldots] gives the following:

Content:
[MATH: n = − 1: f(4 + 2(− 1))|= f(2) = 0; n = − 2: f(4 + 2(− 2))|= f(0) = 0; n = − 3: f(4 + 2(− 3))|= f(− 2) = 0; ⋮]

---

On the other hand, if we shift the graph horizontally by any distance other than [MATH: 3] (or a multiple of [MATH: 3]), we get a different graph.

Therefore, the period of the function is [MATH: 3.]

Item 8 — Example: Inferring Values of a Periodic Function Given Its Graph

Example Prompt:
The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] is shown below. Given that [MATH: f] is periodic with period [MATH: 4], what is the value of [MATH: f(84)?]

[IMG: /graphics/4250bf9ee2ce9af841aca5d1ecb7be51]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since the period is [MATH: 4,] if we add (or subtract) any multiple of [MATH: 4] from the input, the output stays the same.

So, we can keep subtracting [MATH: 4] from the input until we get to an input that we see in the graph:

[MATH: f(84)|= f(84 − 4); = f(84 − 2 ⋅ 4); = ⋯; = f(84 − 20 ⋅ 4); = f(4); = 0]
